Proudly
proud'lĭ
adv. (with pride; arrogantly; in Scripture, chiefly in the phrase “dealt proudly”, of men setting themselves against God)
Old French prud, valiant, which in English took on the sense of overweening. The Hebrew zud means to boil up, to seethe over — pride as a pot that has risen past its rim.

Biblical Definition

The phrase “dealt proudly” is the Bible's standing formula for a settled contempt of God, and Jethro coins it: “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods: for in the thing wherein they dealt proudly he was above them” (Exo 18:11) — Egypt drowned in the very water she had used to drown the Hebrew children. Hannah warns against it in her song: “Talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth: for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed” (1Sa 2:3). The Levites in Nehemiah's great prayer of confession use it twice, and the second use is the point: God shewed signs and wonders upon Pharaoh, “for thou knewest that they dealt proudly against them” (Neh 9:10) — and then, of Israel herself, “But they and our fathers dealt proudly, and hardened their necks, and hearkened not to thy commandments” (Neh 9:16). The identical charge is laid against Egypt and against the covenant people, in one chapter, in the same words. That is the argument of the whole prayer: God is just in all that is brought upon us, for thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines proudly as with an air of superiority; haughtily; ostentatiously; arrogantly; in defiance of authority.

PROUDLY, adv. With an air of superiority; haughtily; ostentatiously.

2. Arrogantly; in defiance of law or authority.

Talk no more so exceeding proudly. 1 Sam. ii.

Key Scripture

Exo 18:11 — "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods: for in the thing wherein they dealt proudly he was above them."

1Sa 2:3 — "Talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth: for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed."

Neh 9:16 — "But they and our fathers dealt proudly, and hardened their necks, and hearkened not to thy commandments,"

Modern Corruption

Pride has been reclassified as a virtue and adopted as a public banner, while the Christian counterfeit — a doctrinal party that despises everyone outside it — goes largely unnamed.

expand to see more

Pride is the one sin our culture has promoted to a public celebration, and it is worth being precise about what the Bible means by the word, because equivocation runs in both directions. Scripture does not condemn the honest satisfaction of a man in good work — let every man prove his own work, and then shall he have rejoicing in himself alone. What it condemns, in the phrase dealt proudly, is the seething-over of a creature against his Maker: the refusal of the place a man has been given, the hardened neck, the arrogancy out of the mouth. God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace unto the humble, and Proverbs sets a proud look at the head of the list of six things the LORD doth hate. That much is easy for a confessional church to say. The harder word is the one Nehemiah 9 forces, where the same charge falls on Egypt and on Israel in the same chapter, in the same words. A Reformed congregation is not automatically on the humble side of that ledger. The doctrines of grace, of all doctrines, ought to make a man least able to look down on anyone — who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? — and where they have instead produced a party that despises the ignorant, the charismatic, the Arminian, and the unlearned, that is not orthodoxy. It is dealing proudly, and Hannah's warning is addressed to it: by him actions are weighed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew zud (H2102), to boil up, to seethe, to act presumptuously; ga'on (H1347), majesty, and so arrogance; Greek huperephanos (G5244), showing oneself above others.

expand to see more

Hebrew zud (H2102) — to boil up, to act presumptuously or proudly; the standing verb of the phrase “dealt proudly”, of Egypt and of Israel; Exodus 18:11, Nehemiah 9:10, 9:16.

Hebrew ga'on (H1347) — exaltation, majesty, and so arrogance; pride goeth before destruction; Proverbs 16:18, Isaiah 2:12.

Greek huperephanos (G5244) — appearing above others, haughty; God resisteth the proud, quoted twice from Proverbs 3:34; James 4:6, 1 Peter 5:5.

Usage

"“In the thing wherein they dealt proudly he was above them” — Egypt drowned in her own instrument."

"“Talk no more so exceeding proudly…by him actions are weighed” — Hannah's song."

"“They and our fathers dealt proudly” — the same charge, the same chapter, the covenant people."
